newsitem.title: POLAND: New Polish constitution clears final legal hurdle.
newsitem.headline: New Polish constitution clears final legal hurdle.

text.p: Poland's Supreme Court on Tuesday ruled that a May referendum which approved the country's new constitution had been valid -- clearing the way for the controversial charter to become law.
"The constitutional referendum of May 25, 1997 is valid," the court's president Jan Wasilewski told a news conference.
PAP news agency quoted President Aleksander Kwasniewski as saying in the flood-hit city of Wroclaw that he would sign the document into law on Wednesday.

The constitution, replacing a Stalin-era one and interim arrangements made since the 1989 fall of communism, was the result of a compromise between government and opposition parties now in parliament. It is strongly criticised by the Catholic Church and its powerful political allies.
The Supreme Court examined the referendum after various citizens raised objections to the way it was conducted. But it found that none of these issues affected the outcome.
It rejected arguments that more than 50 percent of voters should have taken part for the referendum to be valid, saying a vote on a new constitution was different from any other.
In the referendum, the constitution passed by about 53 percent to 46 but only 42.9 percent of voters took part.
The constitution's backers said the document, designed to enshrine liberties won with the fall of communism, is Western in style and embraces people of all faiths or none.

But the church condemned the document for failing to include a clause effectively banning abortion, which is now legal in Poland but could be severely restricted by another separate court ruling earlier this year.
Among other arguments, critics attacked the new constitution for not underlining the close association between Poland's majority Christian faith and its national identity.
The pro-Church Solidarity trade union and allied parties campaigned to reject it in the referendum and surprised even themselves by the narrowness of the majority in favour.

The Solidarity Election Action (AWS) has promised to try to amend the document if it defeats the dominant ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) party in September 21 parliamentary elections and win power.

Solidarity leaders have also argued that the constitution betrayed national interests by allowing Poland to surrender by treaty some functions to international organisations -- provisions designed to ease membership of the European Union.

The constitution's defenders said it is a modern, Western-style document which can embrace people of all religious faiths or none, and leaves room for a tightened abortion law if parliament so decides.
